newsitem.title: USA: Florida approves super-majority tax restriction.
newsitem.headline: Florida approves super-majority tax restriction.

text.p: Florida overwhelmingly approved a proposal requiring two-thirds voter approval for statewide tax increases, a move that virtually assures the state will never have an income tax.
The super-majority amendment passed with 69.3 percent of the votes in Tuesday's election, state officials said.

"We're ecstatic," said Phil Steger, a volunteer coordinator with the TaxCap Committee that collected enough voter signatures to put the constitutional amendment on the ballot. "We're here to protect Floridians from excessive taxes and regulations. It's designed first and foremost as a protection against a state income tax."

Income taxes are prohibited by the Florida Constitution. The super-majority amendment, which was Amendment One on Tuesday's ballot, would make it harder to change that. Steger said the sponsors were thrilled with their wide margin of victory.
"For us to achieve that two-thirds majority ourselvs was more than we could have hoped for. A two-thirds majority is not an onerous requirement for something as drastic as an income tax," he said.
Next year, Steger said, the TaxCap group will seek a similar amendment imposting the same super-majority requirement for state and local tax increases.
"This is going to scare the bejeebies out of our state representatives," he said.

In other statewide referendums Tuesday, Florida voters approved a proposal requiring pollutors to pay for clean-up efforts in the Everglades, and another establishing an Everglades Trust Fund to act as a conduit for state and local clean-up money.

But Florida voters rejected a fiercly contested proposal to levy a penny-a-pound tax on sugarcane growers to fund Everglades clean-up. Farmers have been blamed for allowing fertilizer-laden water to run off their fields into the sensitive wetlands.
Sugar growers, who previously agreed to pay up to $300 million over the next 20 years for Everglades clean-up, said the new tax would have cost jobs and put some smaller growers out of business.
The tax proposal failed with 54.1 percent of voters voting against it, and 45.6 percent voting for it.

Florida voters also approved an amendment calling for the next Constitutional Revision Commission to begin its review in 1997 instead of 1998 as previously scheduled, and giving the panel more leeway in recommending changes to the state constitution.
